notes.meaning: Jesus explains that the Father has given all authority and truth into His hands. The Father and the Son share a deep, complete knowledge of one another that no human can have on their own. We can only truly know God when the Son chooses to reveal Him to us.

differ.view: Teachers in this tradition view this through the hidden God versus the revealed God, showing that God outside Christ is hidden and terrifying, but in Jesus He makes Himself known as a gracious Savior.
Believers in this tradition highlight that Jesus knows the Father with total divine knowledge, and any knowledge people receive of God is entirely a gift of His sovereign grace.

notes.meaning: Turning privately to His disciples, Jesus calls them deeply blessed because of what they are witnessing. They were seeing God's promised salvation and kingdom breaking into the world right before their eyes.

Many faithful leaders of old, including great prophets and kings like David, longed to see the Messiah and hear His words. Those early believers only saw God's promises from a distance, but Jesus' disciples were experiencing them firsthand.

An expert in religious law stood up to test Jesus and see how sound His teaching was. He asked what action he needed to take to inherit eternal life, which means living forever in God's heavenly kingdom. He treated salvation like a reward to be won through a single great deed.

Jesus answered the expert by asking him what was written in the Scriptures and how he understood it. As a teacher of the law, the man already knew the commands God had given. Jesus wisely placed the question back on the man's own field of study.

The expert answered by quoting two famous commands from the law of Moses: to love God with all one's heart, soul, strength, and mind, and to love one's neighbor as oneself. The first part came from the Shema, a prayer faithful Jews recited every single day. Together, these two commands sum up everything God requires.

Jesus told the man that his answer was completely correct. If anyone could live out this perfect love without failing, they would truly live. Jesus upheld the standard of God's law to show that true love must be proved in action.

differ.view: Many evangelicals teach that Jesus gave this answer not to show that good deeds earn salvation, but to expose that no human can keep the law perfectly, driving the sinner to depend on grace.

notes.meaning: Wanting to prove he was righteous and blameless, the man asked Jesus who counted as his neighbor. People in that culture often limited neighbor to fellow Israelites and excluded outsiders. The lawyer was looking for a boundary line so he could feel confident that he had kept the rule.

Jesus answered by telling a story about a traveler walking down the steep, rocky road from Jerusalem to Jericho. That lonely route through the desert was famous for bandits who hid along the hills. Robbers attacked the traveler, stripped off his clothes, beat him severely, and left him half dead.

A Jewish priest happened to travel down that very same road. Priests were religious leaders who conducted worship and offered sacrifices to God in the temple. Yet when he saw the battered man, he crossed the road and passed by on the other side.

A Levite also came down the road and reached the exact same spot. Levites were temple assistants who helped the priests carry out sacred duties in God's house. Although he came up and looked at the wounded man, he too walked past on the opposite side.

A Samaritan on a journey came upon the injured traveler. Jews and Samaritans were longtime rivals who disliked and avoided each other deeply. Yet when the Samaritan saw the dying stranger, he felt deep pity and compassion for him.

The Samaritan went over to the stranger, bandaged his injuries, and poured on oil to soothe the pain and wine to clean the wounds. He then placed the man on his own animal and walked alongside him to an inn. There he spent the night watching over him and caring for his needs.

The next morning, the Samaritan gave two silver coins to the innkeeper to care for the traveler. Two denarii equaled about two full days of wages for a worker, which covered several days of shelter and food. He promised to repay any extra expenses when he returned from his trip.

Jesus asked the lawyer which of the three travelers proved to be a real neighbor to the wounded man. The question changed the lawyer's focus from deciding who deserved kindness to asking what kind of person shows genuine love. Real neighborliness is revealed when someone steps forward to help a person in distress.

The legal expert had to admit that the true neighbor was the one who showed mercy, though he avoided saying the name Samaritan. Jesus then commanded him to go and do the same. God calls His people to show generous mercy to anyone in need, even to enemies.

As Jesus and His followers traveled on toward Jerusalem, He entered a village named Bethany. A woman named Martha opened her home and welcomed Him with warm hospitality. As the mistress of the house, she took charge of receiving her guests.

Martha had a sister named Mary, who sat quietly at the Lord's feet to listen to His words. Sitting at a teacher's feet was the traditional posture of a devoted disciple. In that time, rabbis rarely took women as disciples, but Jesus welcomed Mary as a learner.

Martha was pulled in many directions and felt stressed by all the serving work. Upset that she had to handle the preparations alone, she stepped forward and asked Jesus if He cared that her sister had left her to work by herself. She demanded that Jesus tell Mary to get up and help.

The Lord answered with warmth and tenderness by repeating Martha's name twice. He pointed out that she was troubled and weighed down by many household duties. Her good desire to serve had turned into inner worry and outer stress.

Jesus told Martha that only one thing is truly necessary. Mary had chosen the best portion by sitting to hear God's word, and that spiritual gift would not be taken away from her. Household duties have value, but feeding on God's truth must come first.

differ.view: Reformed Christians emphasize that Jesus was not calling Martha's service evil, but was making a comparison to show that receiving Christ's teaching is the far better thing.
Lutheran teaching stresses that Jesus was not rebuking the duty of loving one's neighbor, but recognizing human limits and pointing to hearing God's word as the primary blessing.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view Martha and Mary as examples of two different leadership ministries in the early church, hospitality and discipleship, rather than comparing housework with spiritual life.
